purpose: Mesna is given to protect your bladder from damage that can be caused by certain chemotherapy drugs, especially ifosfamide and cyclophosphamide. It works alongside your cancer treatment to prevent a painful and potentially serious condition called hemorrhagic cystitis, which is bleeding in the bladder. Think of it as a shield for your bladder during chemotherapy.
how_it_works: When some chemotherapy drugs break down in your body, they create a harmful byproduct called acrolein that can irritate and damage the lining of your bladder. Mesna travels to your bladder and binds to acrolein, making it harmless so it can be safely flushed out in your urine. It does not interfere with how your chemotherapy works against cancer cells.
common_side_effects: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, stomach cramps, headache, tiredness, flushing, and a bad or unusual taste in your mouth. Some people may notice their urine has a slight odor, which is normal.
warnings: Tell your doctor right away if you notice blood in your urine, since this could mean bladder irritation is still occurring. Let your healthcare team know if you are allergic to mesna or any similar compounds. If you have an autoimmune condition, mesna may rarely cause reactions. Always tell your doctor about all medications and supplements you are taking before starting mesna.
typical_dosing: Mesna is usually given by injection into a vein (IV) at specific time points around your chemotherapy doses — often right before and then again 4 and 8 hours after chemotherapy. In some cases, it may be given as tablets by mouth. Your doctor or nurse will schedule the exact timing based on which chemotherapy drugs you are receiving. It is important not to miss doses for the best protection.
